title: Dai Hi Shin Dharani
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona's main teaching emphasizes that true understanding and liberation come not from intellectual comprehension of spiritual concepts, but rather from direct experience and awareness. Through meditation and practice, we can cultivate a deeper connection to the present moment, allowing us to transcend our individual boundaries and limitations. This is where "Buddhas" or enlightened beings appear in life, guiding us towards a more profound sense of unity and understanding.

sentences.text: Maybe it didn't expect us to study Buddhism from Oprah magazine.
There's no place it does not reach.
Meditate and lose weight.
I'm afraid maybe it won't be able to come back, because I can't afford to lose weight.
Our hearts are with Tim this evening as he has gone to be with his family in Seattle, who are confronting the greatest of mysteries: the mystery of birth and death.
So this talk will be a continuation in our series of talks as we're working through our chant books.
The topic of tonight's talk is the Daihishin Dharani.
Shall I start with a translation of what the Japanese mean when they're chanting this chant, into English?

The first line is "Namu kara tan no tora ya ya namu or ya boryo ki chi shifu ra ya", and what this means to the Japanese as they're chanting is "Namu kara tan no tora ya ya namu or ya boryo ki chi shifu ra ya".
So it's a bunch of sounds, just a bunch of sounds to them, actually.
The original text was in Sanskrit, and the Chinese wrote down the sounds they heard when it was being chanted in Sanskrit.

Then the Japanese wrote down the sounds they heard when they heard the Chinese chanting it, and then we wrote down, using Arabic characters, the sounds that we heard when we heard the Japanese chanting what the Chinese had been chanting.
Now a mantra is a short phrase used as the object of meditation.
A commonly used one in Zen would be "gate gate para gate parasamgate bodhisvaha", and if you are undertaking a practice of using that mantra, you would make that the object of meditation.
Every breath in, maybe even just a piece of it: "bodhisvaha" on the inhale, "bodhisvaha" on the exhale.
So a mantra, after practicing a while with it, even if it's in English, loses its meaning as we traditionally understand it and actually takes on meaning in all meaning.
Similar to the way that we practice with the breath, we can practice with language.
Often in Zen, well, in fact koan practice, which is more associated with the Rinzai tradition but is certainly widespread in the Soto tradition also, the student takes the crux of the koan.
We hear these long, confusing koans, and we take the turning point and breathe that phrase again and again.
Under Tim's guidance I practiced a while with the story of Ananda's "yes".
Ananda was called and he responded "yes", and that was a turning point in his enlightenment.
So it was just practicing again and again, every breath, with "yes".
So that's what a mantra is.
Now a Dharani: there are a few Dharanis in our chant book.
Tonight we're talking about the Daihishin Dharani.
A Dharani is basically a long mantra.
So it is the object of meditation, and the meaning really is not the point.
What we call the Daihishin Dharani is chanted throughout Buddhism, throughout the origins of Buddhism in the Asian countries: Tibet, Korea, Vietnam, China, Japan, all schools of Buddhism.
It's commonly referred to under its Sanskrit name, which is the Nilakantha Dharani.
The sounds are different enough that you can be sure that what we are chanting sounds such that the original speakers in Sanskrit probably wouldn't understand it.
It has been kept in translation as [unclear: "a minor study"], which is a praise to Avalokiteshvara in the translation of our tradition.
That translation maybe happened 1200 years ago.
Originally it was a speech by Avalokiteshvara.

According to the Maha Karunikachitta Sutra, Avalokiteshvara spoke before a great assembly, including thousands of Buddhas, and basically made praises to universal understanding, to, in fact, specific Hindu deities.
Ming Zhen Shakyam points out that it's kind of like the Christian tradition picked up practices like Sunday from the religions that it displaced.
The Daihishin Dharani Sutra basically picked up its meaning in Buddhism from the religions that it displaced, although it didn't so much displace Hinduism, for sure.
So the point is sounds, and paying attention to the sounds in our body as we chant the sutra.
That really means paying attention.
Speaking of paying attention, I'm sorry if this blue light is distracting you.
I have the phone on to do the recording and I hope it's not distracting.
I don't know how to shut it off.
There have been a few translations into English over the years, maybe D.T.
Suzuki being one of the early ones.
I will talk about the translation by the Soto Shu, which is the international organization rooted in Japan that organizes, is the arbiter, maybe, on Soto Zen.

Our tradition, in the lineage of Suzuki Roshi and the San Francisco Zen Center, does value highly the pronouncements of the Soto Shu organization, not necessarily following step by step, but taking it very seriously.
And this is actually a good translation.
I looked at a few of them, and the Soto Shu translation is fairly complete.
So this was the original meaning.
I take it back.
This is the Zen tradition meaning of the translation of the Daihishin Dharani.
*Adoration to the triple treasure*, which is of course a reference to the three refuges, Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
*Adoration to Avalokiteshvara, the Bodhisattva Mahasattva, who is the Great Compassionate One.
Aum to the one who performs a leap beyond all fears.
Having adored him, may I enter into the heart of the blue-necked one known as the noble, adorable Avalokiteshvara.
It means the contemplating of all meaning.
It is pure.
It is that which makes all beings victorious and cleanses the path of existence.
Thus, Aum, the seer, the world-transcending one.
Oh Hari, the Maha Bodhisattva.
All, all.*
*Defilement, defilement, the earth.
The earth, the earth.
It is the heart.
Do, do the work.
Hold fast, hold fast.
Oh great Victor, hold on, hold on.
I hold on.
To Indra, the creator.
Move, move, my defilement-free seal.
Come, come, hear, hear.
A joy springs up in me.
Speak, speak, directing.
Hulu, Hulu, Mala.
Hulu, Hulu, Hile.
Sera, sera, sere, sere, sere, sere.
Be awakened, be awakened.
Oh merciful one, blue-necked one.
Of daring ones, to the joyous, hail.
To the successful one, hail.
To the great successful one, hail.
To the one who has attained mastery in the discipline, hail.*
*To the blue-necked one, hail.
To the boar-faced one, hail.
To the one with the lion's head and face, hail.
To the one who holds a weapon in his hand, hail.
To the one who holds a wheel in his hand, hail.
To the one who holds a lotus in his hand, hail.
To the blue-necked, far-causing one, hail.
To the beneficent one, referred to in this Dharani, beginning with Nama.
Hail.
Adoration to the triple treasure, adoration to Avalokiteshvara, hail.
May these prayers be successful.
To this magical formula, hail.*
Well, that's pretty self-explanatory.

The blue-necked one is a reference to Shiva, who was known as blue-necked because some of the minor deities in the Hindu tradition were seeking power and ended up, as a byproduct, creating this poison that had the ability to destroy the world, kind of like corporate America today, maybe.
Shiva took the poison and drank the poison to save the world, and so he is known as the blue-necked one because he has the poison in his throat.
The one who carries the poison of the world, maybe, is the way that Avalokiteshvara is the one who hears the cries of the world.
Very strong correlation there.
The lion-faced one maybe is a reference to, and the boar-faced one to, incarnations of Vishnu.
The lion-faced one is the Narashima, the protector incarnation of Vishnu, and the boar-faced one is maybe a reference to Vahara, another incarnation of Vishnu.

As we noted before, blue-necked was Shiva, so Shiva, Vishnu, and Brahma together in Hinduism are referred to as the Hindu trinity, the three as one, basically all understanding, all that there is, are these three.
So actually, the Oprah article isn't that bad.
Not bad at all.
We talked about how our focus of meditation is usually the breath, and here is a study of using sound, chanting, as a focus of meditation.

The author of the Oprah article is talking about using an exercise from mindfulness-based stress reduction, which is the maybe non-sectarian clinical application of meditation that Tim teaches in his other life now.
In this particular exercise, the object of meditation is being a mountain, imagining being a mountain.
What the article points out is that when we practice being aware of our mental patterns and desires, but not acting on them immediately, we tend to get a little better at it.
Not much surprise there.
We practice things to get better.
In a way, that's a lot of what we're doing in meditation: being aware of what comes up and not necessarily acting on it.
So being aware of food cravings, for example, that come up, and not acting on them.
Now, of course, that doesn't mean that in a year we can overcome all of our cravings.
I practiced tuba for over a dozen years and I never got particularly good at it.
So just practicing something doesn't necessarily make us masters.
But I was certainly a heck of a lot better at the end of those 12 years than I was when I started.
So we practice, and we don't depend entirely on ourselves, as if there was an "ourselves" that we could depend entirely on.
We try to connect with what's greater than ourselves and lose some of the distinction between inside and outside.
And Buddhas tend to show up in life, everywhere.
There was a time, working at the hospital, that I was on the elevator with my tool cart, trying to get up to a higher floor.
On the elevator with me was a small elderly housekeeper who didn't speak much English, and a couple of young x-ray technicians pushing some complicated piece of equipment.
The elevator got up from the ground floor to the first floor and the door opened, and there was a patient in a bed there, with somebody pushing the bed, wanting to get on to get the patient up.
So I moved up to the one wall to make room, and the x-ray technicians spun around and moved over to the other wall.
Then we realized that wasn't going to work, so I tried to get off the elevator to make room, but the bed was right in the way and so I couldn't get off.
At the same time the x-ray technicians decided to push the piece of equipment over to the other side, but it was getting caught.
The housekeeper is standing there watching this like some Tom and Jerry cartoon.
After she had her amusement she said, "You."
She pointed to me.
Pointed to the corner.
Okay, so I backed up into the corner.
She pointed to the x-ray technicians, pointed to the wall, and they scooched over to that wall, and then she scooched in with me, and the bed came on, and on we went.
How do these Buddhas show up?
So I'm going to close with a quote from the Hidden Transmission of the Lamp.
*The laywoman Yu Daopo made doughnuts for a living.
She also studied Chan with Master Linji, who told her to contemplate Linji's phrase "the true person of no rank"* as part of a koan.
As part of a koan.
As a mantra.
Losing its meaning.
Gaining meaning.
Basically losing its distinction from its own meaning with the rest of the meaning.
*The true person of no rank.
One day she and her husband were delivering doughnuts.
And as they walked through the street they met a beggar who was singing "happiness in the lotus land."* Imagine that.
*Yu was suddenly enlightened and she threw the tray of doughnuts to the ground.
Her husband scolded her, "Have you gone crazy?"
She slapped him, saying, "This is not a realm you understand."* Now, what you could read that is, "this is not a realm you understand."
But I think it's, "this is not a realm you understand."
*She then went to see Linji, who immediately verified her awakening.
One day after this Linji asked the assembly, "Which one is the true person of no rank?"
Yu shouted out this verse: "There is a true person of no rank who has six arms and three heads.
When she uses her full strength to cut Mount Hua, it is split in two.
Her strength is like the ever flowing water, not caring about the coming of spring."*
